g.text: uint32 — covers type, seq, len AND payload
uint8 — PUT=1 | DELETE=2 | CHECKPOINT=3 (reserved, never written); 0 invalid
uint64 — strictly increasing; gaps ok, repeats refused
uint32 — refused vs file size + MaxRecordBytes before any alloc
[]byte — opaque to wal; PUT = ver | idLen | id | dim | float32s | metadata
uint16 — present from the first byte written

div.p: crc32c over the header too — a corrupt length is the dangerous one: it turns a bad read into an arbitrary allocation. Nothing is allocated on a length that has not been bounded.
Type 0 is invalid — zero-filled space never decodes as a record.
version — a format without one can never be migrated.
seq — tells replay where the snapshot ends and the tail begins.
The graph is derived state, never the source of truth. It can always be rebuilt from snapshot + log. That is what makes the write ordering non-negotiable.
Fail closed: the first WAL error makes the DB permanently ErrReadOnly (a DurabilityFailure event); reads keep working.
Under SyncInterval / SyncNever an acknowledged write may still sit in the user-space buffer — a process crash can lose it too.

g.text: The decision in the snapshot — settled
Snapshot file — 16 B header + payload + 12 B trailer
uint64 — checksummed; wins over the file name
streamed — gigabytes, never held in memory
uint64 — cross-checked against the file size

div.p: A segment is deletable once the next segment's first seq, read through the checksummed reader, is ≤ the oldest retained snapshot's seq + 1. Never the newest segment. Truncating against the newest snapshot would strand the older copy.

g.text: Recovery — Open, the only time the WAL is read

div.p: Why a new segment: appending after a torn tail would bury good records behind a permanent stopping point. The one reuse is a newest segment that is exactly an 8 B header. FirstSeq = max(N+1, replay's NextSeq).

div.h3: Tested by actually killing the process
div.p: TestCrashMidWriteKeepsEveryAcknowledgedRecord spawns a child, SIGKILLs it mid-write, reopens, and asserts every acknowledged record survived. TestAnotherProcessIsRefused does the same to prove the kernel drops a dead holder's flock.

g.text: 6 · Verify the OLDEST retained, then wal.Truncate(oldest.Seq+1)

div.h3: Serialize the graph, not just the vectors
div.p: Measured at 1M × 128: verifying and decoding the graph is ~0.36 s; re-inserting every vector is ~506 s on one core — about 1,400×.
The price: the codec freezes node on disk, so changing it is a format migration (TestCodecLayoutIsFrozen).

g.text: 1 · snapshot.Load — newest that verifies end to end
2 · Install graph + metadata at seq N
6 · Tear ends the SEGMENT, not the replay

div.p: fsync the old segment before creating the new one, whatever the sync policy — otherwise a crash leaves a hole in the middle of the log, the one shape recovery cannot repair.
fsync the directory on every new segment, or a crash can take a fresh segment — and SyncAlways writes inside it — away.
MaxSegmentBytes is a truncation granularity, not a size cap. ~9 ms per rotation amortizes to 0.29 µs/record. Segments sort numerically, never lexically.

g.text: skipped if nothing logged or compacted since the last one

div.p: payload = GVDB header · graph section (hnsw WriteTo) · metadata section (store.Map) — self-delimiting, sharing one bufio.Reader on load

only after the new one is durable
exclusive for a writer, shared for WithReadOnly
corrupt → SnapshotRejected, try the older one
dimension, metric or M differ → refused
the log no longer reaches back — restore the snapshots
runs of PUTs via InsertBatch, flushed at every DELETE

div.p: Logical truncation (bytes stay on disk), a TornLog event, then on to the next segment — a twice-crashed log has a tear in the middle, and that is normal.

append FIRST, then apply (writeMu; applyMu for the apply only)
